background: An online shop runs a banner ad on paid social and wanted a better headline for its spring campaign. Three new headlines were written: a **Savings headline**, a **Speed headline** and a **Social-proof headline**. Each ran against the **current banner**, with impressions split evenly within each of three audiences: new visitors, returning visitors and subscribers. The example is fictional, made to show how an ad test reads as a report.

Only the ad platform's totals exist: how many people saw each version, how many clicked, how many of those bought, and the revenue per visitor who clicked. No individual visit was exported, so every number is a total the platform reported.
story.intent: The marketing lead asked: “Which headline should the spring campaign run, and for whom?” A headline is only worth running where it brings in purchases, not just clicks.
questions: Does any new headline turn more of the people who click into buyers than the current banner, in any audience?
Do more clicks come with more purchases, or can a headline raise clicks without raising sales?
Is the answer the same for new visitors, returning visitors and subscribers?
story.rule: Fixed before the campaign: roll a headline out to an audience only if at least 5% of the people who click it buy (the break-even point), and the interval for its difference from the current banner stays above zero, so the gain is unlikely to be chance.

alternatives.control: The current banner, already running; every new headline is measured against it.
alternatives.v1: The Savings headline: a new headline built around saving money.
alternatives.v2: The Speed headline: a new headline built around speed.
alternatives.v3: The Social-proof headline: a new headline built around other customers. It ran for new and returning visitors only, not for subscribers.

cases.s1: New visitors, 60,000 impressions per version: people who have not bought before, where a headline has the most to win.
cases.s2: Returning visitors, 30,000 impressions per version: people who know the shop, to see whether a headline still matters to them.
cases.s3: Subscribers, 15,000 impressions per version: the shop's most loyal audience, where a change could also lose sales.

story.covers: Clicks per impression, purchases per click and revenue per visitor who clicked, for each version in each audience, as the ad platform totalled them.
story.notCovered: Individual visits, repeat purchases after the first, the cost of the ads themselves, other channels than paid social, and the Social-proof headline's effect on subscribers, where it did not run.

glossary.meaning: Clicks divided by impressions: how often people who saw the ad clicked it.
Purchases divided by clicks: how often people who clicked went on to buy.
The difference between two rates: 6.3% against 4.1% is 2.2 points.

decision.headline: Run the **Savings headline** for new visitors on paid social, and keep the **current banner** everywhere else.
detail: For new visitors the Savings headline turned 98 of 1,560 clicks into purchases (6.3%) against 47 of 1,140 (4.1%) for the current banner. The gain of about 2 points stays above zero and the rate clears the 5% break-even.
No other headline and segment pair did both. The Speed headline raised clicks among returning visitors (3.4% of impressions against 2.8%) without raising purchases.

limits: Only the platform's totals exist, so how revenue varied between visitors cannot be shown. The platform's own interval is drawn where it gave one; every other interval is computed from the counts.

The pooled rows in Results and Difference mix the three segments unevenly, because the Social-proof headline never reached subscribers, who buy most: its pooled purchase rate reads below the current banner's for that reason alone. Read the segments, not the pool.
Eight variant-and-segment comparisons with the current banner were read. The one clear gap should be repeated before the budget moves.
The Social-proof headline was not shown to subscribers, so that cell is missing, not zero.

sections.title: Purchases among new visitors
sections.label: New visitors
sections.lead: The difference the rollout rests on, read inside the one segment it applies to.
sections.reading: Inside the new-visitor audience the Savings headline's purchase rate is 2.2 points above the current banner's (interval +0.4 to +3.8): the one difference in the campaign that clears both parts of the rule.

readings.compared: Four versions of the banner: the current one and three new headlines. Only the headline differs; each version was shown to the same three audiences.
readings.results: Across all audiences the Savings and Speed headlines drew more clicks than the current banner (3.1% and 3.1% of impressions against 2.7%), but their purchase rates were about the same (7.3% and 7.0% against 6.9%). The Social-proof headline drew fewer clicks (2.4%), fewer purchases (5.4%) and less revenue per visitor ($4.06 against $5.12).
readings.differences: Against the current banner, the Savings headline added 0.4 points of clicks (interval +0.26 to +0.54) and the Speed headline 0.3, both clear of zero; neither added purchases that clear zero (Savings +0.4 points, interval −0.9 to +1.6). The Social-proof headline did worse on all three measures, each interval below zero.
readings.cases: The audiences answer differently. Among new visitors the Savings headline turned 98 of 1,560 clicks into purchases (6.3%) against 47 of 1,140 (4.1%) for the current banner; among returning visitors and subscribers no headline beat the banner's purchase rate by more than chance.
readings.observations: Thirty-three totals, three measures for each version in each audience it ran in; the Social-proof headline has none for subscribers because it did not run there.
